changes.before: Turn typed name-and-score pairs into display labels.
changes.after: Give each position in a pair a clear type and meaning.

before: A string[] describes an array whose elements are strings. Its length can vary.
A tuple describes positions with specific types. The type [string, number] requires text at position 0 and a number at position 1.
A readonly tuple rejects assignment to its positions through that typed reference. It does not freeze external data at runtime.
For the exercise, format ["Mira", 8] as "Mira: 8". Map every row in order. Do not swap the two positions or change the supplied list.
after: An array such as string[] holds text items and can have different lengths.
A tuple describes each position separately. In `[string, number]`, position 0 must be text and position 1 must be a number.
Readonly stops assignments to the tuple's positions through this type. It does not freeze outside data while JavaScript runs.
`const [unit, amount] = row` gives local names to the two positions. This is called destructuring. The labels in the tuple type help readers; they do not create object properties such as row.unit.

Map calls a callback for each array item and collects its results into a new array in the same order. ReadonlyArray<ScoreRow> means the supplied list cannot be changed through that reference. Read each row to make a new label.
For the project, turn each name-and-score pair into text such as Mira: 8. Keep the row order and leave the supplied list unchanged.

before: Read each tuple by position or destructuring.
Return one label per row without changing the input.
after: Read each row's name and score by position or destructuring.
Use map to return one new label per row.
